title: Brighton Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Brighton well records show a 66-ft median depth, 13.6 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $9,300-$16,600.
h1: What Brighton Well Records Mean for Your Property
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Brighton means looking past the well permit and asking what the local records can actually tell you. Within 5 miles of Brighton, Colorado, Adams County, DWR records include 6,023 permitted wells. Of those, 3,394 are recorded as constructed, 3,654 report total depth, 1,323 report pump yield, and 271 report a static water level.

This area is on the plains and sits over Denver Basin aquifers. The local record includes shallow wells, deep wells, domestic supplies, irrigation wells, and monitoring wells, so the numbers are useful for screening a property but do not replace a site-specific well evaluation.

sections.heading: Brighton well depth varies sharply across the plains
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Brighton is 66 feet. The middle half runs from 36 to 440 feet, which is a wide spread for a buyer trying to budget a new well. The 90th percentile is 724 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,378 feet.

Depth mix explains the variation: 53% of wells are under 100 feet, 10% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 23% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 13% are 600 feet or deeper. A driller should not price a lot from the median alone. Ask for a written bid with a per-foot rate, casing and grout assumptions, pump setting, and a clear treatment of extra depth.

sections.heading: Brighton well yields are generally workable, but verify the test
sections.html:
The reported median pump yield is 13.6 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. In the available yield records, 54% produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 45% produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 1% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 0% are reported under 1 gallon per minute.

That is a useful local picture, not a guarantee for a particular lot. Yield reports may represent different test methods and well uses. Confirm the permit, production test, pump information, storage tank, and intended household demand before assuming a well can support a house, irrigation, or livestock.

sections.heading: Brighton water levels show a mixed historical record
sections.html:
The median static water level is 20 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 10 to 94 feet. That suggests many local wells encounter water relatively close to the surface, but the broad range matters for casing, pump setting, trenching, and construction planning.

The decade series does not show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was 38 feet in the 1960s, 44 feet in the 1980s, 260 feet in the 1990s, 35 feet in the 2000s, 18 feet in the 2010s, and 16 feet in the 2020s. The 1990s value is notably different from the surrounding decades. Treat these as reported measurements from a limited group of wells, not a site-specific forecast.

sections.heading: Permit history reaches from Brighton’s older wells to 2025
sections.html:
Brighton has a long drilling history. Permits issued by decade were 223 in the 1950s, 291 in the 1960s, 726 in the 1970s, 543 in the 1980s, 870 in the 1990s, 1,012 in the 2000s, 749 in the 2010s, and 350 in the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2025.

Domestic and household wells make up 51% of the use mix. Monitoring wells account for 20%, irrigation 11%, and stock 8%, so not every nearby record represents a home water supply. The most active named drillers are Authorized (Pe, Pg), John'S Drilling Inc. (John, Lloyd), and Roger Schocke Well Drlg. Inc. (Schocke, Roger). Use these records as local history, not as a recommendation.

sections.heading: A Brighton well budget starts with depth, not just the pump
sections.html:
For the Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock described in the local cost model, drilling commonly runs $50 to $70 per foot. At the 66-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $3,300 to $4,600. A finished well, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is modeled at about $9,300 to $16,600.

Those figures are planning numbers. A deeper-than-median well can change the budget quickly, and access, casing, grout, power distance, water storage, and difficult excavation can add work. Have the contractor separate drilling from completion equipment and site work. Confirm what happens if the hole is deeper than the estimate or does not produce an acceptable supply.

sections.heading: Check water quality, low yield, and septic constraints before closing
sections.html:
Environmental screening deserves attention around Brighton. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 669 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3 historic mine features, and 13 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A mapped site is not proof that a private well is contaminated, but it is a reason to review the location and test the water through a qualified laboratory.

Also check for low production, an unsuccessful hole, pump condition, and the distance between the well, septic system, drainfield, property lines, and proposed building area. Colorado DWR permits control the authorized use. Exempt household-use wells have a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin. Review water rights before designing irrigation or additional uses.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Brighton, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Brighton is 66 feet. The middle half ranges from 36 to 440 feet, while 13% of reported wells are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest record is 1,378 feet. Nearby results vary substantially, so use neighboring permits to frame a bid rather than treating 66 feet as a guaranteed drilling depth.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Brighton?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 66-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $3,300 to $4,600. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $9,300 to $16,600. A deeper hole, difficult access, or extra site work can move the actual bid higher.

faq.q: How much water do Brighton wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 13.6 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Records show 54% producing 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 45% producing more than 15 gallons per minute. Those figures vary by well and test method, so request the specific well’s production test before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Brighton, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or a nearby yield record. Within about 10 miles, the mapped environmental inventory includes 669 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3 historic mine features, and 13 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory and review nearby environmental information before relying on it for household use.

faq.q: Can I use a Brighton well for a house and irrigation?
faq.a: The permit controls the authorized use, so do not assume a domestic well includes irrigation. Nearby records are 51% domestic or household, 11% irrigation, 8% stock, and 20% monitoring. Exempt household-use wells have a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses. Review the permit and water rights before planning irrigation.
